Rural Appalachian counties carry a disproportionate diabetes burden, since 232 of 420 Appalachian counties fall inside the CDC's "Diabetes Belt," and West Virginia alone has roughly 15% of its population diagnosed with diabetes and another 35% classified as prediabetic.
[shard_03741_84635]
Residents of the region's economically distressed counties are about 1.4 times more likely to have diabetes than people in non-Appalachian counties, and among 45-to-64-year-olds the rate is roughly 1 in 5 in distressed counties versus 1 in 8 elsewhere, showing that place-based poverty drives much of the local excess risk.
[shard_04098_50176]
Nationally, diabetes prevalence is also sharply unequal by race and ethnicity, with diagnosed prevalence highest among American Indian/Alaska Native adults at 14.7%, followed by Hispanic adults at 12.5% and non-Hispanic Black adults at 11.7%, compared with 7.5% among non-Hispanic white adults.
[shard_04146_24253]
For a coalition whose county may be largely white but deeply poor, the practical lesson is that income and place, layered onto whatever local racial or ethnic disparities exist, are the fault lines to track when targeting outreach and measuring equity.
[shard_04098_50176] [shard_04146_24253]
On top of higher prevalence, rural communities face a real access gap: 62% of rural counties have limited access to diabetes self-management education and support, even though rural populations have higher diabetes rates than urban ones, and common barriers include geographic isolation, lack of transportation, and lower health literacy.
[shard_03669_83262] [shard_03741_84635]
That combination, higher need plus thinner services, is exactly why a small grant can have outsized impact if it targets the access gap rather than duplicating existing infrastructure.
Among the five options, the evidence base is strongest, and most mutually reinforcing, for community health workers (CHWs) and diabetes self-management education and support (DSMES).
DSMES itself has solid evidence: participation is linked to improved diabetes knowledge, lower A1C, lower costs, and better quality of life, and the American Diabetes Association's Standards of Care treat it as a top-tier recommendation.
[shard_00868_77795]
The problem is uptake, not efficacy: only 5–7% of people eligible for DSMES through Medicare or private insurance actually receive it nationally, and that gap is worse where rural access is limited.
[shard_00868_77795] [shard_03669_83262]
CHWs are among the best-evidenced ways to close that gap in a resource-poor rural setting: a randomized controlled trial in American Samoa found that patients receiving home-visit CHW support were twice as likely as usual-care patients to achieve a clinically significant A1C improvement over one year.
[shard_00493_64689]
In West Virginia's own Mingo County, a CHW program under the Appalachian Diabetes Control and Translation Project followed more than 100 high-risk patients and cut their average A1C from 10% to 7.5% in six months.
[shard_04098_50176]
CHWs are explicitly endorsed by the ADA Standards of Care as a "cost-effective, evidence-based strategy" that has succeeded specifically in "rural and hard-to-reach communities," and low-cost models exist: the HELP PD trial paid trained community members only about $100 a week, later $200 a month, to lead weight-loss groups, with researchers now testing Medicaid reimbursement for this approach.
[shard_02658_6395] [shard_04070_50099]
Because CHWs can deliver home visits, reinforce DSMES content, help with transportation, screen for prediabetes and food insecurity, and refer people into the National Diabetes Prevention Program, they function as connective infrastructure that makes every other program work better, which is why they should be the coalition's first investment.
Screening and prediabetes classes through the National DPP have excellent standalone efficacy: structured lifestyle-change programs that achieve 5–7% weight loss and 150 minutes per week of activity cut progression to type 2 diabetes by 58%, and by 71% for people over 60, with a 10-year follow-up showing participants remained about one-third less likely to develop diabetes.
[shard_00392_75212]
But that program only helps people who are already identified, referred, and retained through a year of sessions, so launching a class without a referral and outreach mechanism risks low enrollment; the Appalachian project needed CHWs and mini-grants just to recruit 132 DPP participants across ten counties.
[shard_00392_75212] [shard_04098_50176]
That argues for sequencing DPP or screening classes as a close second priority, built on top of a CHW referral pipeline, rather than launching classes in isolation.
Food pantry partnerships should rank above broad built-environment projects, because the evidence distinguishes food insecurity from mere physical food access: a widely cited study found that adding a supermarket to a low-access neighborhood did not meaningfully reduce A1C.
[shard_02174_40243]
By contrast, produce-prescription programs pairing food distribution with clinical referral produced measurable gains in a pooled analysis of nine US programs, where participants' A1C fell, blood pressure and BMI improved, and self-reported food insecurity dropped by about a third.
[shard_00978_29218]
This suggests a modest grant is better spent funding a food-pantry or produce-prescription partnership tied to CHW or clinical referral than funding a stand-alone grocery, transit, or sidewalk project whose link to glycemic control is far less certain.
[shard_02174_40243] [shard_00978_29218]
Built-environment and broader food-access infrastructure work still matters, and Appalachian coalitions have used it as a policy lever, with 96% of the region's coalitions improving public facilities for physical activity and 75% working on hunger-related food access.
[shard_04098_50176]
But because these projects are capital-intensive, slower to show clinical results, and dependent on matched funding and multi-year commitment, they fit better as a second-phase, leveraged-funding goal, pursued once the coalition can point to early wins to attract matching grants, exactly as Appalachian coalitions grew local match dollars from about $110,000 in 2011 to nearly $1 million by 2015.
[shard_04098_50176]
For the commissioners, the practical priority order is therefore: fund a CHW workforce first, since it is the cheapest, most rural-adapted, and best individually evidenced lever available.
Pair it immediately with DSMES access, including telehealth delivery, and DPP or screening referral pathways so the CHWs have somewhere to send people they identify.
Layer in a food-pantry or produce-prescription partnership tied to that same referral system, because it treats food insecurity, the outcome-linked problem, more efficiently than physical food access alone.
[shard_02174_40243] [shard_00978_29218]
Finally, treat larger built-environment or food-access construction projects as a longer-horizon initiative pursued through matching funds and regional partnerships, rather than the first draw on a modest, one-time grant.
[shard_04098_50176]
